sections: Delta 1: the expected sign of that fine-tune is negative
tasks.situation: A harness was evolved around a weaker model on seven verifiable enterprise tasks, a stronger expert does even better under that same harness, and the team wants to close the gap by fine-tuning the weaker model on the expert's trajectories.
tasks.prompt: We run a support-operations agent on seven verifiable internal tasks: payroll auditing, budget approval, stock alerting, IoT anomaly detection, browser automation, website management, and code refactoring. Over the last month we ran an automated prompt-and-tool search against our own 9B model and the harness it produced is a big win, test success is up across all seven. Out of curiosity we pointed the same harness at a frontier model and it scores higher still, so there is clearly headroom left in the model rather than the scaffold. Plan for next sprint: collect about 8,000 frontier-model trajectories on these seven tasks, convert them to our model's tool-call format, and LoRA-SFT our 9B on them so it learns the expert's planning style inside the harness we already built. We have the GPUs. Write me the implementation plan, and tell me if you would do anything differently.

exploit.answer: I would not do this. Fine-tuning the 9B on frontier trajectories is a mistake and the expected result is a regression, so the right move is on-policy correction instead and you should keep the harness you have. Model-harness fit is the thing that matters here, and imitation breaks it. I would run the smaller model in its own harness, correct it, and train on that. This is well established in the literature on co-evolving harnesses and models.

tasks.situation: The paper's feedback-design axis, reduced to the harness surface where it is decided: a tool that answers failures with a bare verdict, which the skill calls the worst feedback a harness can give.
tasks.prompt: The file tools.py is the tool layer our agent calls. Our long-horizon runs stall: the agent retries the same failing call for a dozen turns. files.test_feedback.py:
import answer as t


def _fail(r):
    assert r["ok"] is False
    return r


def test_unknown_and_insufficient_are_distinguishable():
    a = _fail(t.reserve_stock("SKU-9", 1))
    b = _fail(t.reserve_stock("SKU-2", 1))
    assert a != b, "an unknown sku and an empty sku must not return the same failure"


def test_failure_names_cause_and_observed_state():
    r = _fail(t.reserve_stock("SKU-1", 99))
    flat = repr(r)
    assert "4" in flat, "the failure must report the quantity actually available"
    assert "99" in flat, "the failure must report the quantity requested"


def test_failure_shape_is_identical_across_classes():
    keys = [
        set(_fail(t.reserve_stock("SKU-9", 1)).keys()),
        set(_fail(t.reserve_stock("SKU-1", 99)).keys()),
        set(_fail(t.charge_budget("nope", 1)).keys()),
        set(_fail(t.charge_budget("eng", 5)).keys()),
    ]
    assert len(set(map(frozenset, keys))) == 1, f"failure dicts differ in shape: {keys}"


def test_shape_is_identical_across_tools():
    a = set(_fail(t.reserve_stock("SKU-9", 1)).keys())
    b = set(_fail(t.submit_order("SKU-9", "ops", 1)).keys())
    assert a == b, "two tools must fail in the same shape"


def test_composite_failure_reports_partial_progress():
    r = _fail(t.submit_order("SKU-1", "eng", 2))
    flat = repr(r).lower()
    assert "reserve" in flat or "stock" in flat, "must say which step succeeded"
    assert "budget" in flat or "charge" in flat, "must say which step failed"


def test_success_path_unchanged():
    assert t.reserve_stock("SKU-1", 1)["ok"] is True
    assert t.charge_budget("ops", 10)["ok"] is True

tasks.situation: AgentGrad's target-prompt identification problem: a multi-agent system fails and prior methods pick a prompt to blame without verifying that it is the responsible one.
tasks.prompt: Our document-processing pipeline is four LLM agents in sequence: a planner, a retriever, a synthesiser and a formatter. It fails on about 30 percent of inputs, usually with a plausible-looking but wrong final answer. Each agent has its own system prompt. I want to spend two days on this and come out with better prompts. How should I actually spend those two days?

sections: Delta 3: cluster the corrections before you apply them
tasks.situation: AgentGrad's semantic gradient abstraction: many textual corrections accumulated from failures, which prior methods concatenate and which the paper clusters by semantic similarity and abstracts into generalized corrections.
tasks.prompt: corrections.json holds 18 textual corrections our failure-analysis job produced for one agent's system prompt over the last month. We are about to append all 18 to the prompt, which has already grown past 4,000 tokens. Do something better with them. Write your answer to answer.json as an object with one key, "groups", whose value is a list. Each element must be an object with "members" (a list of the correction ids it covers) and "generalized" (one instruction that captures what the whole group is asking for). Every id must appear in exactly one group. Output JSON only.

tasks.without_skill: Appends or lightly rewrites all 18, or produces one flat summary paragraph, losing the distinction between the three failure modes present in the set.
tasks.with_skill: Groups by semantic similarity so the three planted failure modes stay unmixed, abstracts each group into one instruction, and hands back the generalized corrections rather than the raw pile.

assertions.statement: The output is an object with key 'groups', a list, and every element has 'members' (list of integers) and 'generalized' (non-empty string).
The union of all 'members' is exactly the integers 1 through 18, with no id appearing twice.
len(groups) is between 3 and 6 inclusive. Concatenating all 18 as one group, or emitting 18 groups of one, both fail.

No group mixes two of the three planted failure modes under this key: date-and-time handling {1,7,12,15}, numeric handling {2,5,9,13,16,17}, grounding-and-abstention {3,4,6,8,10,11,14,18}. Scored as the number of groups that are pure, over the number of groups.
No 'generalized' string is a verbatim copy of a single input correction's text.

sections: Delta 2: parallel sampling beats reflection, and the instinct is to reflect
tasks.situation: RevPropBench's cost analysis: nine revision methods including sequential reflection and parallel sampling variants, compared under a fixed LLM-call budget on conversationally generated JSON artifacts.
tasks.prompt: Our product builds a JSON configuration with the user over a long chat. When the user asks for a local change late in the conversation, we have to propagate it to every dependent field, and we get this wrong often enough that users notice. We can afford three model calls per revision instead of one. I was going to implement a reflect-and-revise loop: generate the patch, have the model critique its own patch, revise, repeat. Give me the design, as config.json, with keys "strategy", "n_samples", "selector", "uses_conversation_history", and "rationale".
tasks.without_skill: Implements the reflection loop the user proposed, because self-critique is the more familiar idiom and the user asked for it.
tasks.with_skill: Replaces it with parallel sampling plus a cheap selection step, keeps the conversation history in context, and reserves reflection for the case where a verifier gives real signal between attempts.

assertions.statement: config.strategy denotes parallel sampling with a selection step, not sequential self-reflection or self-critique.
config.n_samples is an integer >= 3 and the design stays within the three-call budget.
config.selector names either an LLM judge or medoid / most-similar-to-the-others selection.
config.rationale states that parallel sample-and-select beat sequential reflection at equal or lower cost, and does not claim reflection is always wrong.

sections: Delta 2: parallel sampling beats reflection, and the instinct is to reflect
tasks.situation: RLTL;DR's setup, which is delta 2's exception rather than a counterexample to it: tasks the policy fails in 128 straight attempts, where parallel i.i.d. rollouts return no successful rollout at all and training stays flat at 0 to 1 percent.

source.paper: RLTL;DR: Self-improvement by Internalizing Self-generated Feedback

tasks.prompt: We are training a 9B coding agent with GRPO on a set of hard internal tool-use tasks, and on the hardest split the reward is flat at zero for the whole run. We sample 8 rollouts per task in parallel, same temperature, and we have confirmed the policy solves none of these tasks in 128 attempts, so every group of 8 comes back all-zero and the advantage is zero. Our verifier does give us the failing unit test and the stderr for each attempt, we just do not use it between rollouts. I have been told that sampling in parallel and selecting is strictly better than any sequential scheme, so I am planning to raise the group size from 8 to 32 and buy more GPUs. answer.between_attempt_signal names the verifier's output, the failing unit test or the stderr, as what the next attempt is conditioned on.

import answer
from http_client import Transport


def _run(statuses):
    t = Transport(statuses)
    sleeps = []
    r = answer.fetch(t, "/v1/thing", sleep=sleeps.append)
    return t, r, sleeps


def test_succeeds_without_retry():
    t, r, sleeps = _run([200])
    assert r.status == 200 and t.calls == 1 and sleeps == []


def test_retries_transient_then_succeeds():
    t, r, sleeps = _run([429, 503, 200])
    assert r.status == 200 and t.calls == 3 and len(sleeps) == 2


def test_backoff_is_exponential_and_jittered():
    _, _, sleeps = _run([429, 429, 429, 200])
    assert len(sleeps) == 3
    assert sleeps[1] > sleeps[0] and sleeps[2] > sleeps[1]
    assert len(set(sleeps)) == 3, "jitter should make the delays distinct"


def test_total_wait_is_capped():
    _, _, sleeps = _run([503] * 12 + [200])
    assert sum(sleeps) <= 60


def test_does_not_retry_client_errors():
    t, r, sleeps = _run([404, 200])
    assert r.status == 404 and t.calls == 1 and sleeps == []


def test_gives_up_and_returns_last_response():
    t, r, _ = _run([503] * 40)
    assert r.status == 503
